Wherever the term “aircraft” is used, it refers to both aeroplanes and rotorcraft. The performance standards were derived from ICAO Document 9625 Edition 3 Volume 1 and 2, with some modifications based on an analysis of single and multi-engine; multi-crew coordination and Instrument Procedures Check requirements from and CAR Part IV training program requirements. The technical requirements and evaluation criteria specific to aeroplane and rotorcraft FSTDs are presented in the following appendices and tables: A. (2) The MSP may delegate recurrent evaluations of Level 1 and 2 FTDs to Regional Authorities after the NSEP completes the initial evaluation and follow-up corrective action. The expression “generic device” has traditionally been used to designate such non-type-specific devices; however, in this chapter, the expression “generic device” has been replaced by “non-type-specific” to preclude confusion with the simulation feature fidelity as defined by the Table 6.2-1 below. Note: Class” in relation to the classification of aircrafts, means aircrafts having similar operating characteristics to single-engine aircrafts, multi-engine aircrafts, centre-line thrust aircrafts, land aircrafts or sea aircrafts. Note: Set of Aircraft” is a group or series of aircraft group that share similar handling and operating characteristics, similar operating envelopes, and have the same number and type of engines or powerplants. These devices are not authorized for any experience, training or checking credits in type-specific approved training programs. MCC and IPC training or checking on FTDs simulating aeroplanes that require a type-rating may only be conducted on type-specific FTDs (See para 6.4.3 for eligible FTDs) (2) There are two basic non-type-specific FTD configuration: (3) (a) Level 1 - A level 1 FTD is the lowest fidelity device and may have a “generic” cockpit design. The device does not require a visual system or active force-feedback flight controls. It will support basic instrument procedural training, and may provide experience credit for 5 hours pursuant to CAR 421.26(4)(a) pending evaluation. (b) Level 2 – A Level 2 FTD, is a device that represents a “designated” class and set of aircraft. The device requires active force-feedback flight controls and requires a visual system that meets the minimum requirements in Tables E1A or F1A as applicable. It will support basic instrument procedure training and may provide experience credit for 10 hours pursuant to CAR 421.30(4)(a)(ii)(A)(III) pending evaluation. An aeroplane FTD may qualify for instrument proficiency checks (IPC) and/or for multi-crew coordination (MCC) training in an ATP(A) program if the device meets the following criteria. (a) MCC Qualification. An FTD may qualify as a Multi-Crew Coordination FTD provided that it: (i) Meets the criteria objective and subjective test criteria for an FTD Level 2, 5, 6, or 7; and

IPC Qualification. An FTD will qualify as a platform to conduct Instrument Proficiency Checks (IPC) provided that it: (a) Meets the criteria objective and subjective test criteria for an FTD Level 2, 5, 6, or 7; (b) Meets or exceeds the criteria outlined in Appendices E for the IPC qualification; and (c) Fully supports the procedural and operational performance tasks IPC in the Advisory Circular AC-401-004 as amended to conduct an IPC. Note: An aeroplane FTD granted an additional MCC or IPC qualification will be designated on the FSTD certificate as Level #-MCC. (i.e. Level 5-MCC; Level 2-IPC; Level 6-MCC/IPC) Note: The term “Designated” is used when a feature or requirement must be specifically identified by the sponsor prior to the initial evaluation or update evaluation. (5) Detailed standards and tests for the various levels of FTDs are fully defined in Appendices E for aeroplanes and Appendices F for rotorcraft. 6.5 General Design Standards (1) To avoid any delays in the design, build, acceptance, or qualification process, the sponsor should engage in early discussions with the TPAA and Approving Authority to broadly agree on the “designated aircraft configuration” and any additional qualifications (MCC or IPC) intended. (2) Cockpit/Flight Deck Configuration. The Sponsor should choose a configuration that sensibly represents the aircrafts likely to be used in the approved training program. To ensure a good training environment, the cockpit/flight deck should be located in a training environment that minimizes any distractions. (a) (b) Level 1. The cockpit/flight deck must sufficiently represent a class of aircraft to support approved use. The cockpit/flight deck may be open or enclosed. The appearance, arrangement, operation, and function of physical switches and other required controls must be realistically placed. The instrument panel of an aeroplane FTD must include at least the following: (i) Master/battery; (ii) Magnetos for each engine (as applicable); (iii) Alternators for each engine; (iv) Fuel boost pumps for each engine; (v) Avionics master; (vi) Pitot heat; and (vii) Rotating beacon/strobe, navigation, taxi, and landing lights. Level 2. The cockpit/flight deck must be representative of a set of aircrafts or the aircraft itself to support approved use. The cockpit/flight deck must be sufficiently enclosed to minimize distractions. The physical arrangement, appearance, and operation of controls, instruments, and switches should model at least one aircraft in the family of aircraft represented as closely as practicable.

Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards (3) Page 6-5 Cockpit/Flight Deck Components. Physical flight and aircraft system controls must be recognizable as to their function and how they are to be manipulated solely from their appearance. (a) Physical flight and aircraft system controls must not use interfaces such as a keyboard, mouse, or gaming joystick to control the represented aircraft in simulated flight. (b) Components used within the cockpit/flight deck area do not need to be aircraft parts; however, any parts used should be representative of typical training aircrafts and should be robust enough to endure the training tasks. (c) The use of simple flat display technology-based representations and touch-screen controls to represent objects other than basic push-button types of controls will not be acceptable. The training tasks envisaged for these devices are such that appropriate layout and feel is very important. For example, the altimeter sub-scale knob needs to be physically located on the altimeter. The use of flat display technologies with physical overlays incorporating operational switches/knobs/ buttons replicating an aircraft instrument panel may be acceptable. 6.6 Data package (1) The data for the aerodynamics model, flight controls and engines used in Level 1 or 2 FTDs must be based on sound engineering principles and substantiated in the form of a “Reference Data” engineering report (RDR). The RDR shall show that the proposed validation data are representative of the aircraft or the class of aircrafts modelled. This report may include flight test data, manufacturer’s design data, information from the aircraft flight manual (AFM) and maintenance manuals, results of approved or commonly accepted simulations or predictive models, recognized theoretical results, information from the public domain, or other sources as deemed necessary by the FTD manufacturer to substantiate the proposed model. (2) Generic or representative data may be derived from a specific aircraft within the class of aircrafts simulated, or it may be based on information from several aircrafts within a group of aircrafts that reflect the performance of the “designated aircraft configuration”. (3) With the concurrence of the NSEP, the data may be in the form of a manufacturer’s previously approved set of validation data for the applicable FTD. The sponsor should submit the intended validation data together with a substantiation report to the NSEP for review and approval prior to procurement or the commencement of the manufacturing or procurement process. Once the set of data for a specific FTD has been accepted and approved by the NSEP, it will become the validation data that will be used as reference for subsequent recurrent evaluations with the application of the stated tolerances. (4) Data Collection and Model Development. A basic requirement for any modelling is the integrity of the mathematical equations and models used to represent the flying qualities and performance of the aircraft or class of aircrafts being simulated. The models should be continuous and vary sensibly throughout the required training flight envelope. The following principles apply: (a) Additional data to refine the non-type-specific model can be obtained from many sources, such as aircraft design data, flight and maintenance manuals, observations on the ground and in the air, etc., without necessarily having to conduct expensive, dedicated flight testing. (b) Data obtained on the ground and in flight can be measured and recorded using a range of simple means such as video cameras, paper and pencil, stopwatch, and new technologies (e.g. GPS). (c) Data gathering should take place at representative masses and centres of gravity. Development of such a data package including justification and the rationale for the design and intended performance, the measurement methods and recorded parameters

(5) Flight Controls. There can be a strong interaction between the flight control forces and the effects of both the engines and the aerodynamic configuration and will reflect the fidelity and credits offered to the FTD: (a) Level 1 FTDs only require “generic” fidelity level flight controls, which may be achieved with a passive force cueing system utilizing springs. The evaluator will assess the fidelity of the flight controls during the initial and recurrent evaluations. Qualification will not be awarded if the flight controls manifest any characteristics that would result in negative training. (b) Level 2 FTDs require “representative” fidelity level flight controls, which will require an active force feedback cueing system that allows flight controls forces to vary with position as well as aircraft configuration (speed, flaps, trim). 6.7 Visual System (1) The adequacy of the performance of the visual system will be determined by its ability to support the intended training tasks, e.g. “visual cueing sufficient to support changes in approach path by using runway perspective”. (2) Collimated visual optics are not required for non-type-specific FTDs since no training credits for landing are available. A single channel direct viewing system is acceptable for level 2. For MCC and IPC additional qualifications, the visual FOV must be as per Appendix E2 (applicable to aeroplanes FTDs only). (3) Where the device does not simulate a particular aircraft type, the design of the out-ofcockpit/flight deck view should be matched to the visual system so that the pilot has a FOV sufficient for the intended training tasks. For example, during an instrument approach the pilot should be able to see the appropriate visual segment at decision height. Additionally, where the aircraft deviates from the normal approach path, undue loss of visual reference should not occur during the subsequent correction. 6.8 Transport Delay (1) For a non-type-specific device, a transport delay test may be used to demonstrate that the FSTD system does not exceed the permissible delay. However, for such a device using simple models, a Statement of Compliance (SOC) may be acceptable in lieu of a test. The SOC must contain a system block diagram that support a description of the cumulative latency or transport delay from control input to instrument, visual and motion system response as applicable. The SOC should also describe the method of determining the transport delay. (2) The maximum permissible transport delays is 300 milliseconds for aeroplanes and 120 milliseconds for rotorcraft. A test may be required during the initial evaluation to verify the SOC if the calculated transport delay is close to the maximum permissible value. 6.9 Testing/Evaluation (1) To ensure that any device meets its design criteria initially and periodically throughout its life, a system of objective and subjective testing will be used. (2) The validation tests specified in Appendix E2 for aeroplanes and Appendix F2 for rotorcrafts will be flown by a suitably skilled person and the results recorded manually. (3) Automatic Recording and Testing. The MSP must be notified if a sponsor wishes to use automatic recording and testing for validation tests. In such a case, the QTG review will be

(4) (5) (6) The tolerances specified are designed to ensure that the device meets its original target criteria year after year. It is therefore important that such target data are carefully derived and values are accepted by the NSEP or Regional Authority in advance of the initial evaluation (QTG review). Unlike the target parameters stipulated for type-specific devices, those stated for non-type-specific FSTDs are primarily intended to ensure repeatability during the life of the FSTD and in particular at each recurrent regulatory inspection. For initial qualification, the device should meet its design criteria within the listed tolerances; however, the evaluator may approve reasonably altered target values if they do not adversely affect the performance of the FTD or the quality of training and the results are repeatable. A number of tests within the QTG have had their tolerances reduced to “Correct Trend and Magnitude” (CT&M) thereby avoiding the need for specific validation data. The use of CT&M is not to be taken as an indication that certain areas of simulation can be ignored. For such tests, the performance of the FSTD should be appropriate and representative of the simulated aircraft and should under no circumstances exhibit negative characteristics. Where CT&M is used as a tolerance, it is strongly recommended that a simple, reliable, and repeatable test method be designed to establish a baseline result approved during the initial evaluation. This will be provide a means of avoid or resolving any divergent subjective opinions during recurrent evaluations. Longitudinal change force tests. For Level 1 and 2 aeroplane FTDs, it is acceptable to use change force tests instead of the longitudinal power, flap and gear change dynamics tests. The purpose of these change force tests is to simply reproduce the control force feeling during recurrent evaluations. These tests should be conducted in the following way: (a) Trim the aeroplane in straight and level flight in the most suitable configuration; (b) Initiate the configuration change (power, flap or gear change); (c) Maintain the airspeed constant using the pitch control (or as an alternate procedure, maintain the altitude of the original trimmed conditions); and (d) Measure the required pitch control force change. Note: If automatic testing is used, a change dynamics test is acceptable. For each FSTD, the sponsor must submit a “letter of intent” requesting an initial qualification evaluation to their Regional Authority no later than 120 days prior to the evaluation date requested. The letter will include: (i) A description of the FSTD; (ii) The anticipated qualification level of the FSTD; (iii) The make, model, and series of aircraft simulated; and any other pertinent information; and (iv) Any additional information that may affect the scope of the evaluation (i.e. FSTD relocation, sponsorship change, restoration after voluntary suspension etc.) Note: To avoid any qualification delays, the sponsor should contact the MSP as early as possible to coordinate a review and acceptance of the validation data package. (2) Regional Authority’s Response. The Regional Authority will liaise with the MSP to determine the most appropriate evaluation agency (NSEP or Regional Authority). The designated evaluating agency will reply to the letter of intent within 15 business days with the following information; (a) Tentative dates for the initial evaluation; (b) The date the sponsor must submit the QTG if applicable;

The Sponsor will submit the QTG and the Reference Data Report (RDR) in a form and manner described in this chapter. The evaluating agency will review the QTG and forward comments and questions resulting from the review to the Sponsor for their response. Depending on the results of the review, the designated evaluating agency will confirm or postpone the evaluation date. The sponsor will provide a response to the QTG review comments no later than 5 working days before the evaluation date. (4) Letter of Compliance. The Sponsor will submit a “letter of compliance” signed by the management representative no later than 5 working days before the evaluation confirming that: (a) Qualified pilot(s), after having flown all of the applicable subjective evaluation in the applicable QPS appendix tests (Table E1B for aeroplane FTDs) relevant to the qualification level of the FSTD, have determined that the performance and handling qualities of the FTD represent those of the class or set of aircraft within the normal operating envelope. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. The name of the pilot(s) making this determination must be identified on the letter of compliance. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (b) Qualified pilot(s) or person(s) trained on simulator systems/sub-systems and trained on the operation of the simulated aircraft systems, after having exercised the operation of the FTD and the pertinent functions available through the Instructor Operating Station(s), have determined that the FTD cockpit configuration, systems, and sub-systems (including the simulated aircraft systems) functionally represent those in the aircraft class or set of aircraft. The name of the person(s) making this determination must be available to the MSP upon request. Exceptions, if any, must be noted. (c) When the FSTD passes an evaluation for initial qualification, the MSP issues a Qualification Certificate as described at paragraph 6.2.3 of this chapter. (5) After the NSEP completes the evaluation for initial qualification, the sponsor must update the Qualification Test Guide (QTG), with the results of the TC-witnessed tests as determined by the evaluator. For the purposes of this manual, an FSTD is said to have been modified when: (a) Equipment or devices intended to simulate aircraft appliances are added to or removed from the FSTD, which change the MQTG or the Qualification Certificate issued by the Minister; or (b) Changes are made to either software or hardware that; (i) are intended to impact flight or ground dynamics; (ii) that impact performance or handling characteristics of the FSTD (including motion, visual, control loading, or sound systems for those FSTD levels requiring sound tests and measurements); or (iii) require an amendment to the MQTG. Note: Routine software or hardware changes, or changes to the MQTG which do not affect required objective testing results or validation data approved during the initial evaluation of the FSTD are not considered modifications. Chapter 6 – Non-Ty pe Specific Flight Training Device – Qualification Performance Standards Page 6-13 6.14 Conduct of Initial and Update Evaluation (1) The Regional Authority may only evaluate non-type-specific FTDs for sponsors holding a TC certificate as a Flight Training Unit. The NSEP will evaluate all type-specific FTDs. (2) The evaluator will assess each FTD configuration as completely as possible. To ensure a thorough and uniform evaluation, each FTD will be evaluated against the general simulator requirements in Appendix E1 or F1, the objective tests listed in Appendix E2 (aeroplanes) or F2 (rotorcraft), and the subjective tests listed in Appendix E3 (aeroplanes) or F3 (rotorcraft), as applicable. The evaluations will include, but not necessarily be limited to the following: (3) (4) (a) Aircraft responses, including longitudinal and lateral-directional control responses (see Appendix E2 (aeroplanes) or F2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (b) Performance in authorized portions of the simulated aircraft's operating envelope, to include tasks evaluated by the MSP in the areas of surface operations, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, approach, and landing as well as abnormal and emergency operations (see Appendix E2 (aeroplanes) or F2 (rotorcraft)); (c) Control checks (see Appendix E1 and E2 (aeroplanes) or Appendix F1 and F2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (d) Flight deck configuration (see Appendix E1 (aeroplanes) or F1 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (e) Pilot, flight engineer, and instructor station functions checks (see Appendix E1 and E3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix F1 and F3 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (f) Aircraft systems and sub-systems (as appropriate) as compared to the aircraft simulated (see Appendix E1 and E3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix F1 and F3 (rotorcraft) as applicable); (g) FTD systems and sub-systems, including force cueing (motion), visual, and aural (sound) systems, as appropriate (see Appendix E1 and F2 (aeroplanes) or Appendix E1 and F2 (rotorcraft) as applicable); and (h) Certain additional requirements, depending upon the qualification level sought, including equipment or circumstances that may become hazardous to the occupants. The sponsor may be subject to Occupational Safety and Health Administration requirements. The evaluator will administers the objective and subjective tests, which includes an examination of functions. The tests include a qualitative assessment of the FTD by a TC pilot. (a) Objective tests provide a basis for measuring and evaluating FTD performance and determining compliance with the requirements of this chapter. (b) Subjective tests provide a basis for: (i) Evaluating the capability of the FTD to perform over a typical utilization period; (ii) Determining that the FTD satisfactorily simulates each required task; (iii) Verifying correct operation of the FTD controls, instruments, and systems; and (iv) Demonstrating compliance with the requirements of this manual. In addition to the scheduled continuing qualification evaluation, each FTD is subject to evaluations conducted by the NSEP or Regional Authority at any time without prior notification to the sponsor. Such evaluations would be accomplished in a normal manner (i.e. requiring exclusive use of the FTD for the conduct of objective and subjective tests and an examination of functions) if the FTD is not being used for pilot training and checking. However, if the FTD were being used, the evaluation would be conducted in a non-exclusive manner. The FTD evaluator will accompany the instructor aboard the FTD along with the student(s) and observe the operation of the FTD during the training, testing, or checking activities in a non-interference manner.

(6) After an FTD is evaluated and deemed compliant, the Regional Authority issues a Qualification Certificate to the sponsor. The Certificate is also the Regional Authority’s recommendation to the TPAA that the FTD may be used in a TC approved training program. (7) The numbering system used for objective test results in the QTG should closely follow the numbering system set out in Appendix E2, Table E2A (aeroplanes) or Appendix F2, Table F2A (rotorcraft) as applicable. 6.15 Continuing Qualification Evaluations and Requirements (1) The sponsor must conduct objective tests at least once annually and retain test results and the FTD defect log for at least two consecutive years. (2) During the continuing qualification evaluation conducted by the Regional Authority, the sponsor must also provide a person knowledgeable about the operation of the aircraft and the operation of the FTD. (3) The Regional Authority will ensure the frequency of continuing qualification evaluations is in accordance with the requirements of CAR 606.03 unless the Regional Authority becomes aware of discrepancies or performance problems with the device that warrants more frequent evaluations. (4) The continuing qualification evaluations will normally require 4 hours of FTD time. The sponsor should anticipate that evaluations will consist of the following: (a) Review of the sponsor-conducted objective tests results and defect log. (b) A random selection of objective tests from the MQTG that provide an adequate opportunity to evaluate the performance of the FTD. The tests chosen will be performed manually and should be able to be conducted within approximately one-third of the allotted FTD time. (c) A subjective evaluation of the FTD to perform a representative sampling of the tasks set out in Appendix E3 (aeroplanes) or Appendix F3 (rotorcraft) as applicable. This portion of the evaluation should take approximately two-thirds of the allotted FTD time. (d) An examination of the functions of the FTD may include the motion system, visual system, sound system, instructor operating station, and the normal functions and simulated malfunctions of the aircraft systems. This examination is normally accomplished simultaneously with the subjective evaluation requirements.

Appendix E2 – Aeroplane Non-Type Specific FTD – Objective Tests Page 6-56 Appendix E2 - Aeroplane Non-Type-Specific FTD – Objective Tests (1) In addition to subjective testing, non-type-specific FTDs will be subject to the applicable objective tests at Table E2A to ensure the they meet qualification criteria initially and periodically throughout its life. The objective tests can be flown by a suitably skilled person and the results recorded manually. (2) The tolerances specified are designed to ensure that the device meets its original target criteria year after year. It is therefore important that such target data is carefully derived and substantiated prior to submitting the QTG to the inspecting authority prior to the QTG review and initial qualification. For initial qualification, it is highly desirable that the device should meet its design criteria within the listed tolerances. However, unlike the tolerances stipulated for typespecific devices, the tolerances stated for non-type-specific FSTDs are intended to support recurrent inspection to ensure the device is maintained as approved during the initial evaluation. It is therefore important that the tests targets be representative and test results be repeatable during the life of the FSTD. (3) A number of tests within the QTG have had their tolerances reduced to "Correct Trend and Magnitude" (CT&M) thereby avoiding the need for specific validation data. The use of CT&M is not to be taken as an indication that certain areas of simulation can be ignored. For such tests, the performance of the FSTD should be appropriate and representative of the simulated designated aeroplane and should under no circumstances exhibit negative characteristics. Where CT&M is used as a tolerance, it is strongly recommended that targets are identified and used to footprint the baseline in order to avoid possible divergent subjective opinions during recurrent evaluations. Once a footprint target is established, then the applicable tolerance should be applied to results during recurrent evaluations. (4) Longitudinal change force tests. It is acceptable to use change force tests instead of the longitudinal power, flap and gear change dynamics tests. The purpose of these change force tests is to simply reproduce the control force feeling during recurrent evaluations. If not otherwise stated, these tests should be conducted in the following way: (a) trim the aeroplane in straight and level flight in the most suitable configuration; (b) initiate the configuration change (power, flap or gear change); (c) maintain the airspeed constant using the pitch control (or as an alternate procedure, maintain the altitude of the original trimmed conditions); and (d) Measure the required pitch control force change. Note: If change forces are small (within the tolerance band), it is acceptable to reduce change the end state airspeed to achieve a more measureable force provided the procedure is well documented and repeatable.
